title: Cross-Schema Field Harvesting — Core Method
description: Metadata hides under different field names in every schema — author, creator, byline, committer all mean the same thing — so the harvester maps aliases to canonical metadata slots across any record type, not just media files. It works over database rows, documents, datasets, and file headers with the same alias tables, because authorship and timestamps are universal concepts. Each harvested value keeps its original field name alongside the canonical slot, preserving the audit trail. This general harvesting is what separates a metadata engine from a media-only extractor. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.

title: Timestamp Normalization — Core Method
description: Timestamps arrive in dozens of formats — ISO strings, Unix epochs, 'March 4 2021', database datetimes — and the normalizer converts them all to UTC ISO-8601. Format detection tries strict parsers in order of specificity before falling back to lenient ones, and every conversion records which parser succeeded. Ambiguous dates like 03/04/2021 are flagged rather than guessed, because a wrong date is worse than an unknown one. Normalized time is the foundation of every temporal analysis downstream. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.

title: Authorship Signals — Core Method
description: Authorship is rarely a single clean field: it appears as bylines, commit authors, file owners, and 'last modified by' stamps across different record types. The extractor collects all of these signals and scores them — an explicit author field outranks a filesystem owner — then reports the winner with its evidence. Multiple contributors are preserved as a list rather than collapsed to one name. Honest authorship extraction shows its work, because attribution errors have real consequences. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.
demo:
signals = [("byline", "A. Researcher", 3), ("owner", "sysadmin", 1), ("committer", "A. Researcher", 2)]
best = max(signals, key=lambda s: s[2])
print("author: %s (via %s, weight %d)" % (best[1], best[0], best[2]))

title: Identifier Cross-Linking — Core Method
description: The same work carries many identifiers — a DOI, an arXiv id, a local archive number — and the extractor links them into one identity cluster. Link rules match on identifier schemes first, then on strong metadata agreement like title plus date. Each cluster keeps the full list of equivalent identifiers so any of them resolves to the whole. Cross-linking turns a pile of differently-numbered records into a coherent bibliography. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.
provenance: JAH Databases archive-intelligence tools program, lane T2a — public methods from established computer-science practice.

title: Provenance Consolidation — Core Method
description: Provenance arrives fragmented — a harvest log here, a migration record there, an edit history somewhere else — and the consolidator merges these fragments into one chronological trail per record. Merging keys on record identity and orders events by normalized timestamp, flagging contradictions like two different claimed creators. Gaps in the trail are marked explicitly rather than papered over. A consolidated provenance chain is what lets an archive answer 'where did this come from' with evidence instead of shrugs. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.
demo:
events = [("2021-01-01", "harvested"), ("2021-06-01", "migrated"), ("2020-12-01", "created")]
trail = sorted(events)
print("provenance trail:")
for ts, ev in trail:
    print(" ", ts, "-", ev)
